Inner- City Darkness- Cable Theft

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The City of Joburg has been robbed and plunged into darkness! 6Kms of copper cable was stolen at an estimated value of R240 million Rand. How will the city recover and who's paying the bills?

Summary:
In the past two weeks large parts of the Johannesburg city centre have been affected by electricity power outages that has put a grinding halt to businesses and left residents in the dark.

This is due to a cable thieving syndicate in the inner-city that has led to 6 kilometers of copper cables being stolen from underground tunnels. A number of arrests have been made, and it is believed that members of City Power, possibly contractors, and possibly members of the SAPS all form part of this syndicate. This is a major robbery that will plunge the city into millions of Rands in repair costs.


Further information:
A single meter of copper cable costs around R40 thousand rand, so if 6kms of cable was stolen then the cost of the robbery in cable alone is about R 240 million that the city and of course taxpayers will have to cough up somehow to repair the damage and restore the city. The substation that was burnt will cost City Power R15M to repair.
Although electricity has been restored in many of the areas initially affected by this power outage; there are still some areas in the CBD that are without power. This impacts directly on the day-to-day running of the city’s economy, as businesses have either had to shut down or endure the exuberant costs of keeping shops open through generators.

With the city notoriously known for it’s crimes and unscrupulous night crawlers, the safety of many individuals, particularly women and children could be at risk as the lights out can be an open invitation to more crimes.

In order for this scale of theft to occur it would have had to be a coordinated effort in the nature of a syndicate. How is it that such a large theft can occur and go undetected by the police or City Power? Carte Blanche investigates.

We speak to butcher Joe Dos Reis, who has lost over a million rand in credit card transactions, the cost of running the generators around R16000,00 per day, and they have had to dump 2 tons of wasted stock already this week. They also have to have a permanent security guard at their generator.

Sol Masolo from City power describes for us how the copper cables were stolen and how difficult it is to detect when it is happening, because first City Power has to trace the source of the fault. Some of City power employees are suspected to be involved in these cable thefts, as this has to be an inside job for it to be orchestrated so perfectly, what is City power doing about that? We hope to be taken to the tunnels where the theft occurred and to speak to City Power's investigation and technical unit who will unpack how it is possible to steal that amount of cable, where does it end up? City Power is looking at replacing all copper cable with aluminium cable in the future, as that has no street resale value. But this will be a very costly exercise. They also tell us that they have very strict controls with regard to stock being removed from their stores, but the obvious beneficiaries when this sort of theft happens are the sub contractors, as they are hired to do the repair work, they also have the knowledge of where the cables were laid and this is how the syndicates work.


Wayne Minaar from Johannesburg Metro Police department says some arrests have been made. Is there a way that the police can stop this before it happens next time? Apparently there is a new Infrastructure Protection unit that is being put in place to protect against such crimes, JMPD needs to elaborate on this. What proof is there that this is a syndicate?

Small business owners in the inner city have also been hard hit by the power outages and unfortunately for most unlike the big businesses, they do not have the necessary insurance to cover them for such events. We speak to some Somali business men that run shops in the CBD. How much of a loss has it been for them and can they recover from this?

Allen Mokoki from the chamber of commerce and industry believes this has been a catastrophic situation for business in the city, and not only them but the many more that feed to and from the city. He outlines how this also hurts government as they get to lose on tax as well. Many of the big businesses do not get hard hit by such an event as they usually have plans in place to counter. It’s the small businesses that will feel it the most according to Allen.

We speak to individual residents in the city as they narrate how tough it’s been in the past week and how the have had to cope individually without power for over a week, and how frightened they have been to be out after dark.

Press Release:


In the past two weeks large parts of the Johannesburg city centre have been affected by electricity power outages that has put a grinding halt to businesses and left residents in the dark. The outage was caused by large scale theft with 6Kms of copper cable stolen at an estimated value of R240 million Rand. Who carried out the crime and how? How will the city recover and who's paying the bills?

Script:


VO: This has been the sound of the city of Joburg for almost two weeks. Loud hums from generators dominate the streets signalling - no power

Jo: Our generator is costing us about R15000,00 a day.

Angel: Eish!!! We are stressed because we're going to end yo without any stock, because we don't know when the electricity will come back.
Wayne: The biggest problem was the traffic lights were out.

Link: The city of Joburg was robbed. 6km of copper cable was stolen, plunging the city into darkness

VO: Mayor of Johannesburg, Herman Mashaba says a theft on this scale is tantamount to treason.

Mayor: I think this is one of the biggest treason this country has had to endure. The damage cost to our infrastructure is in excess of R50 Million, but then to really look at the impact to business, I mean must be about 5 times the size.

VO: Jo Dos Reis is a butcher and owns this landmark establishment in the inner-city of Joburg, he has suffered millions of rands in losses and they have a knock on effect.

Jo: I thank God that I'm a bigger business I look at other guys, my neighbors, they are complaining big time, they can't pay the rent. I don't know how a lot of people are going to survive these last two weeks. A lot of businesses won't survive.

VO: This is one of the busiest intersections in the CBD and many people come from outside the city to trade, it is most evident here that over the last two weeks business has virtually ground to a halt. Angel Ndlovu, is just one of the street traders that has been hard hit.

Angel: Business is very slow, There is no business and we are running at a loss. People are not buying, things get wasted, it's too hot so we throw away our stock.

Jo: Well electronic transactions it's over a million Rand. Our clients can't buy because they can't cook. It's really affected us terribly, at least 40 to 50% of our business. Once it's gone it's gone. You can't recover.

VO: But big business, especially corporates were not affected so acutely, they are prepared for eventualities like this, so it’s the people on the ground who will suffer the most.

Jose: You know what I feel the poorer people are even worse affected than us.

Link: This is the kind of cable that was stolen. How does one even begin to steal 6km of this in open sight

Louis: The normal modus operandi is that you make a fire under the cable until the insulation melts. When the insulation melts, it causes a short circuit and when it short circuits you get a trip at your substation.

VO: In the process, a total of 33 kilometers of cable was damaged, according to City Power, Acting director of Engineering and operations Louis Pieterse.

Louis: As an individual you cannot carry out more than 2 and half metres of cable yourself. So you need vehicles, trucks, you've got to take the cable out through a manhole, so you need people, you need lots of hands and you need equipment to remove cables from the tunnels. It cannot just be carried away by individuals.

Link: This is one of the main substations that has been affected by the cable theft. It covers a huge part of Johannesburg. It starts in Maboneng all the way to Bank city

VO: Two main substations were infiltrated on the night of the 3rd of September. Cable insulation was left burning and highly noxious fumes were emitted.

Louis: In the tunnels the cables are oil filled cables at 88000 volt and at 11000v its oil impregnated paper insulation cables. So when the fire starts it doesn't just stop. So you have to clear the tunnel first from a ventilation point of view before you can get in and make sure the fire is killed and if still extinguish the fire before you can do anything else. This whole process took from midnight on Saturday until Tuesday afternoon.

VO: Lucky Sindane, of the Forensics and Investigation Services COJ, tasked with rooting out corruption, says the scale of this operation was enormous.

Lucky: We're dealing with a sophisticated syndicate here. We think that it is people that are involved are from the city in fact and SAPS.

Mayor: We believe very strongly this can not really have been an outside work, we must’ve had inside officials within the city working with them.

Lucky: To get down to the tunnels you must have a map, you cannot just open a man hole and get to the copper cables.

Macfarlane: For someone to get access to this they must have had knowledge. Are there maps involved?

Louis: Indeed there are maps, the information is available we've got maps as City power. It is obviously our city power staff and also the security company that has been assisting us with patrolling the tunnels, but obviously thereby we are not implying that they have been involved. But the information is available and can be leaked

Mayor: This matter came to my attention on monday morning last week and by the evening no arrests made and by that time i had received the extent of the damage. I found it difficult to accept that no arrests have been made. I said it's impossible.


VO: The city then took the difficult decision and offered a reward of 100 000 rand for information on the theft and within hours they had results.

Lucky: During one of our raids that we conducted at a certain scrap yard we received a call from a member of the public who informed us illegal activity that was happening at that scrap yard, He filmed a SAPS marked vehicle collecting money from that scrap yard and leaving.

Mayor: By 2 O' clock members of the community started coming to us. By 4 O' clock 22 people were arrested

VO: Chief Superintendent Wayne Minaar, of the JMPD was present when the arrests were made.

Wayne: I can confirm that 22 suspects have been arrested in connection with cable theft and of the 22, 4 are scrap metal dealers and of the 4, 2 tried to bribe the officers with R10 000. The officers turned down the bribe and we've also added now charge of bribery.

Link: This is one of the four scrapyards where the stolen copper cable was found. A syndicate operating the JHB CBD was bringing the copper in truckloads and transporting it here.

Lucky: The first scrap yard that we went to in Langlaagte we found copper that was stored in drums and in large sacks. They cut it, package it in small amounts that look like money notes. That's what we found in one scrap yard in Langlaagte. They melt it quite small, yes it's easier to transport. In another scrap yard we went to it was still raw they hadn't touched it you know. People who were working there were about to start to work on it, to start peeling off the covers and expose the copper. because they work overnight.

VO: One meter of copper cable depending on the size, costs between R1000 to R2000, on the black market it is sold at R120, to R130,00 per kilogram.


Lucky: The very first that we arrested, a few drums of copper, he bought them for R400 000 just a few drums so imagine what they would've cost

Mac: What do you think happens to all this copper, what's the street value?

Louis: We believe that most if not all, the cable is eventually shipped to China. There is a huge demand overseas. So all this cable at some stage ends up in a container, ends up somewhere at the harbour and eventually ends up in China.

Lucky: The copper cable that was stolen is worth R15million, and we are the unit that made the arrests a day later after the copper cables were stolen so this is our biggest bust as a unit. When it was moved to the police station is took 6, 6 ton trucks.

VO: About 45% of power outages are due to cable theft and the cost to the city has been devastating especially for business owners and residents alike. But the greater cost is to the taxpayer and an additional 25 Million rand will be needed to beef up the current security, so that this kind of crime is minimised.

Louis: The total value of the infrastructure in the tunnel is probably worth about R2 billion. So that's why spending R25 Million on a proper security surveillance system is really a drop in the ocean.

Wayne: There is a Unit which will now be established within the JMPD, to focus mainly on cable theft and there will also be a crime intelligence center set up which will have sophisticated equipment and cameras that will be strategically placed at the locations where there are cables.

VO: It almost appears as though the city of Johannesburg is being held to ransom, plagued with escalating garbage strikes, electricity outages and rampant homelessness, how will the mayor restore order?

Mayor: Criminals it doesn't matter where they come from, whether you're a South African or a foreigner, criminals must be punished.

Macfarlane: Is it a possibility that politics are holding the city to ransom?

Mayor: Absolutely. You don't have to be a rocket scientist, but ultimately people of this city and this country are ultimately going to triumph.

VO: With most of the power restored this week, business is almost back to normal, but the sense of fear still lingers, as darkness descends

JOE: it's scary to be around here at night. We're lucky that some of the lights in the streets work, our corner is very well lit up but most of the corners it's dangerous. Very very dangerous.

FIN!!!!!
ENDS!!!!!!!


PROMOS
PROMO 15”
VO: 6Kms of electrical copper cable was stolen in the Johannesburg city center condemning residents and businesses to darkness for almost two weeks

JOE: It's scary to be around here at night. most of the corners are dangerous. Very, very dangerous.

PROMO 15”
VO: A copper cable stealing syndicate got away with 6km worth of electrical cable and went undetected in Johannesburg’s underground tunnels.

Lucky: You know we're dealing with a sophisticated syndicate here. We think that itis people that are involved are from the city in fact SAPS.

PROMO 10”
VO: A copper cable syndicate looted about 6Km of underground electrical cables in the CBD costing the city of Joburg in excess of 50 Million rand in damage.

PROMOS FIN

I found it difficult to accept that no arrests have been made. I said it's impossible. VO: The city then took the difficult decision and offered a reward of 100 000 rand for information on the theft and within hours they had results. Lucky: During one of our raids that we conducted at a certain scrap yard we received a call from a member of the public who informed us illegal activity that was happening at that scrap yard, He filmed a SAPS marked vehicle collecting money from that scrap yard and leaving. Mayor: By 2 O' clock members of the community started coming to us. By 4 O' clock 22 people were arrested VO: Chief Superintendent Wayne Minaar, of the JMPD was present when the arrests were made. Wayne: I can confirm that 22 suspects have been arrested in connection with cable theft and of the 22, 4 are scrap metal dealers and of the 4, 2 tried to bribe the officers with R10 000. The officers turned down the bribe and we've also added now charge of bribery. Link: This is one of the four scrapyards where the stolen copper cable was found. A syndicate operating the JHB CBD was bringing the copper in truckloads and transporting it here. Lucky: The first scrap yard that we went to in Langlaagte we found copper that was stored in drums and in large sacks. They cut it, package it in small amounts that look like money notes. That's what we found in one scrap yard in Langlaagte. They melt it quite small, yes it's easier to transport. In another scrap yard we went to it was still raw they hadn't touched it you know. People who were working there were about to start to work on it, to start peeling off the covers and expose the copper. because they work overnight. VO: One meter of copper cable depending on the size, costs between R1000 to R2000, on the black market it is sold at R120, to R130,00 per kilogram. Lucky: The very first that we arrested, a few drums of copper, he bought them for R400 000 just a few drums so imagine what they would've cost Mac: What do you think happens to all this copper, what's the street value? Louis: We believe that most if not all, the cable is eventually shipped to China. There is a huge demand overseas. So all this cable at some stage ends up in a container, ends up somewhere at the harbour and eventually ends up in China. Lucky: The copper cable that was stolen is worth R15million, and we are the unit that made the arrests a day later after the copper cables were stolen so this is our biggest bust as a unit. When it was moved to the police station is took 6, 6 ton trucks. VO: About 45% of power outages are due to cable theft and the cost to the city has been devastating especially for business owners and residents alike. But the greater cost is to the taxpayer and an additional 25 Million rand will be needed to beef up the current security, so that this kind of crime is minimised. Louis: The total value of the infrastructure in the tunnel is probably worth about R2 billion. So that's why spending R25 Million on a proper security surveillance system is really a drop in the ocean. Wayne: There is a Unit which will now be established within the JMPD, to focus mainly on cable theft and there will also be a crime intelligence center set up which will have sophisticated equipment and cameras that will be strategically placed at the locations where there are cables. VO: It almost appears as though the city of Johannesburg is being held to ransom, plagued with escalating garbage strikes, electricity outages and rampant homelessness, how will the mayor restore order? Mayor: Criminals it doesn't matter where they come from, whether you're a South African or a foreigner, criminals must be punished. Macfarlane: Is it a possibility that politics are holding the city to ransom? Mayor: Absolutely. You don't have to be a rocket scientist, but ultimately people of this city and this country are ultimately going to triumph. VO: With most of the power restored this week, business is almost back to normal, but the sense of fear still lingers, as darkness descends JOE: it's scary to be around here at night. We're lucky that some of the lights in the streets work, our corner is very well lit up but most of the corners it's dangerous. Very very dangerous. FIN!!!!! ENDS!!!!!!! PROMOS PROMO 15” VO: 6Kms of electrical copper cable was stolen in the Johannesburg city center condemning residents and businesses to darkness for almost two weeks JOE: It's scary to be around here at night. most of the corners are dangerous. Very, very dangerous. PROMO 15” VO: A copper cable stealing syndicate got away with 6km worth of electrical cable and went undetected in Johannesburg’s underground tunnels. Lucky: You know we're dealing with a sophisticated syndicate here. We think that itis people that are involved are from the city in fact SAPS. PROMO 10” VO: A copper cable syndicate looted about 6Km of underground electrical cables in the CBD costing the city of Joburg in excess of 50 Million rand in damage. PROMOS FIN

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The City of Joburg has been robbed and plunged into darkness! 6Kms of copper cable was stolen at an estimated value of R240 million Rand. How will the city recover and who's paying the bills?
metadata.Summary: In the past two weeks large parts of the Johannesburg city centre have been affected by electricity power outages that has put a grinding halt to businesses and left residents in the dark. This is due to a cable thieving syndicate in the inner-city that has led to 6 kilometers of copper cables being stolen from underground tunnels. A number of arrests have been made, and it is believed that members of City Power, possibly contractors, and possibly members of the SAPS all form part of this syndicate. This is a major robbery that will plunge the city into millions of Rands in repair costs.
metadata.Further information: A single meter of copper cable costs around R40 thousand rand, so if 6kms of cable was stolen then the cost of the robbery in cable alone is about R 240 million that the city and of course taxpayers will have to cough up somehow to repair the damage and restore the city. The substation that was burnt will cost City Power R15M to repair. Although electricity has been restored in many of the areas initially affected by this power outage; there are still some areas in the CBD that are without power. This impacts directly on the day-to-day running of the city’s economy, as businesses have either had to shut down or endure the exuberant costs of keeping shops open through generators. With the city notoriously known for it’s crimes and unscrupulous night crawlers, the safety of many individuals, particularly women and children could be at risk as the lights out can be an open invitation to more crimes. In order for this scale of theft to occur it would have had to be a coordinated effort in the nature of a syndicate. How is it that such a large theft can occur and go undetected by the police or City Power? Carte Blanche investigates. We speak to butcher Joe Dos Reis, who has lost over a million rand in credit card transactions, the cost of running the generators around R16000,00 per day, and they have had to dump 2 tons of wasted stock already this week. They also have to have a permanent security guard at their generator. Sol Masolo from City power describes for us how the copper cables were stolen and how difficult it is to detect when it is happening, because first City Power has to trace the source of the fault. Some of City power employees are suspected to be involved in these cable thefts, as this has to be an inside job for it to be orchestrated so perfectly, what is City power doing about that? We hope to be taken to the tunnels where the theft occurred and to speak to City Power's investigation and technical unit who will unpack how it is possible to steal that amount of cable, where does it end up? City Power is looking at replacing all copper cable with aluminium cable in the future, as that has no street resale value. But this will be a very costly exercise. They also tell us that they have very strict controls with regard to stock being removed from their stores, but the obvious beneficiaries when this sort of theft happens are the sub contractors, as they are hired to do the repair work, they also have the knowledge of where the cables were laid and this is how the syndicates work. Wayne Minaar from Johannesburg Metro Police department says some arrests have been made. Is there a way that the police can stop this before it happens next time? Apparently there is a new Infrastructure Protection unit that is being put in place to protect against such crimes, JMPD needs to elaborate on this. What proof is there that this is a syndicate? Small business owners in the inner city have also been hard hit by the power outages and unfortunately for most unlike the big businesses, they do not have the necessary insurance to cover them for such events. We speak to some Somali business men that run shops in the CBD. How much of a loss has it been for them and can they recover from this? Allen Mokoki from the chamber of commerce and industry believes this has been a catastrophic situation for business in the city, and not only them but the many more that feed to and from the city. He outlines how this also hurts government as they get to lose on tax as well. Many of the big businesses do not get hard hit by such an event as they usually have plans in place to counter. It’s the small businesses that will feel it the most according to Allen. We speak to individual residents in the city as they narrate how tough it’s been in the past week and how the have had to cope individually without power for over a week, and how frightened they have been to be out after dark.
